newsitem.title: USA: IMF says capital flows to emerging markets may ebb.
newsitem.headline: IMF says capital flows to emerging markets may ebb.

text.p: Capital flows to emerging market countries may ebb over the next two or three years but will still remain substantial, International Monetary Fund chief economist Michael Mussa said Wednesday.

"We expect that capital flows to emerging market countries in the years to come will remain very substantial," Mussa said at a news conference held for the release of the IMF's World Economic Outlook report.
According to the report, a record $200.7 billion in net private capital poured into developing countries last year, up from last year's $151.2 billion.

The cost of capital to emerging market countries has also declined since early 1995, the report said, especially in Latin America, where spreads on Brady bonds have narrowed considerably in the aftermath of the Mexican peso crisis.
"That being said, whether the level of the capital flows, which last year was very high, will be sustained in 1997 and 1998 is more of a question," Mussa added.
Capital flows to developing countries have been influenced over the past few decades by the behavior of interest rates in industrialized countries.

Mussa noted that in 1996 the industrialized nations had relatively low rates and accomodating monetary policies, adding that the IMF expects a gradual firming of those conditions over the next two or three years.
"And if past patterns hold true, that would have some effect in diminishing capital flows, or in raising the interest costs or interest spreads for a number of emerging markets," he said.
While Mussa assured that he would not expect a dramatic collapse in capital flows, he said some countries may be vulnerable to sudden shifts.
Such countries could run into trouble if their economic policies generate substantial imbalances or if markets start to perceive them in that light.

"There are a few countries, and I wouldn't grade them in this gathering, where we do have some concerns that those conditions may develop and that policy measures to reverse their further development are called for at this time," Mussa said.
Mexico almost caused an international financial debacle late in 1994 by botching a devaluation of its currency after it had spent most of its foreign reserves in a failed attempt to defend the peso.
By then Mexico had run up a massive current account deficit and was largely dependent on capital inflows, stoking market fears that the government would not be able to roll over its short-term debt.
The peso crisis required unprecedented loan packages from the United States and the IMF, which helped Mexico avoid a default on its financial obligations.
